shots.text: That range came from a handful of early radiocarbon and thermoluminescence dates.
shots.desc: old laboratory bench, glassware, sample tins

shots.text: Museum records vary too: the Cleveland Museum of Art gives this head a thermoluminescence date of 20 to 620 CE.
shots.credit: Nok terracotta head · Cleveland Museum of Art (1995.21) · CC0

shots.text: The Frankfurt team began fieldwork in 2005, and from 2009 its long-term project was funded by the German Research Foundation.
shots.desc: grid of excavation squares, string lines, morning

shots.text: They excavated, built a pottery sequence, and gathered more than two hundred radiocarbon dates.
shots.desc: rows of labelled potsherds on a tarpaulin

shots.text: On their chronology, Nok began around 1500 BC.
Its main phase ran from the ninth to the fourth century BC, when terracottas and iron appear.
And it ended around the turn of the Common Era.
The earliest furnace dates fall somewhere between 800 and 400 BC.
shots.desc: glowing clay furnace mouth at night, charcoal

shots.text: But iron smelting by about 800 BC cannot yet be confirmed.

shots.desc: hands pressing wet clay, close up, no face
